Part 1: The Data (2 points)¶

We will be exploring a data set on Women's March Madness (Basketball). This adapted data set contains historical records of every NCAA Division I Women’s Basketball Tournament appearance since the tournament began in 1982 up until 2018. Sourced from official NCAA, the adapted data set captures tournament results across more than four decades of collegiate women’s basketball. All data is sourced from the NCAA and contains the data behind the story The Rise and Fall Of Women’s NCAA Tournament Dynasties.

The data set can be read in from the following url: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diverse-data-hub/diversedata/refs/heads/main/data-clean/womensmarchmadness.csv

To help you with the analysis, here is a table of descriptions of each of the variables present in the model.

Variable Description
year Year
school School Name
seed Seed. The 0 seeding designation in 1983 notes the eight teams that played an opening-round game to become the No. 8 seed in each region.
conference Conference
conf_wins Conference Wins
conf_losses Conference Losses
conf_wins_pct Conference Win Percentage
conf_rank Place in Conference
division Conference Division
reg_wins Regional Wins
reg_losses Regional Losses
reg_wins_pct Regional Win Percentage
bid Whether the school qualified with an automatic bid (by winning its conference or conference tournament) or an at-large bid. [‘at-large’, ‘auto’]
first_game_at_home Whether the school played its first-round tournament games on its home court. [‘Y’, ‘N’]
tourney_wins Tourney Wins
tourney_losses Tourney Losses
tourney_finish Ordered categories: [‘opening_round_loss’ < ‘first_round_loss’ < ‘second_round_loss’ < ‘top_16_loss’ < ‘top_8_loss’ < ‘top_4_loss’ < ‘top_2_loss’ < ‘champ’]
total_wins Total Wins
total_losses Total Losses
total_wins_pct Total Win Percentage

Part 5: Analysis (34 points)¶

In this section, you will describe your data analysis and perform it.

Task 5.1 Plan out your analysis (10 points)¶

Propose a method that was covered in class that would be appropriate to use to answer your research question. You only need to build one model with one set of predictors in this section. Write a paragraph that explains the choice of method, and be sure to answer the following questions:

  • What method do you plan to use?
  • Why is this method appropriate?
  • What are the potential limitations or weaknesses of the method selected?
  • How are you going to process the data to apply the model? For example: Are you splitting the data? How? How many splits? What proportions will you use for the splits? At what stage will you split? Will there be a validation set? Will you use cross validation?
  • How will you assess the performance of the model? Explain why the performance metric(s) chosen ise appropriate.

You answer should be around 250 words or less.

I plan to use K-nearest neighbours classification to answer my research question. This method is appropriate because my outcome variable is binary categorical with two classes representing whether a team advanced or was eliminated, while both tournament seed and regular season win percentage are quantitative predictors. A main limitation of this approach is its sensitivity to the scale of different variables. Tournament seed ranges from 1 to 16, whereas regular season win percentage ranges from roughly 50 to 100. To prevent win percentage from dominating the distance calculations, I will preprocess both predictors using step_scale and step_center in a recipe.

I will partition the data into a 75 percent training set and a 25 percent testing set using initial_split with stratification on the target variable. Within the training partition, I will use five-fold cross-validation with vfold_cv to find the optimal number of neighbours K. Finally, I will evaluate the model on the unseen test set using classification accuracy and a confusion matrix. These metrics are appropriate because accuracy summarizes overall correctness, and the confusion matrix checks whether the model predicts both advancing and eliminated teams effectively.

Task 5.2 Perform the Analysis (20 points)¶

  • Perform the proposed analysis.
  • Be sure to comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow.

You may add more code cells if needed.

In [1]:
library(tidymodels)

# Set seed matching the project notebook for reproducible splitting and CV
set.seed(43449222)

# Split data into 75% training and 25% testing sets, stratified on outcome
march_tidy <- mutate(march_tidy, advanced_first_round = factor(advanced_first_round))

march_split <- initial_split(march_tidy, prop = 0.75, strata = advanced_first_round)
march_train <- training(march_split)
march_test <- testing(march_split)

# Build preprocessing recipe to normalize both numeric predictors
march_recipe <- recipe(advanced_first_round ~ seed + reg_wins_pct, data = march_train) |>
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

# Create 5-fold stratified cross-validation folds on the training data
march_vfold <- vfold_cv(march_train, v = 5, strata = advanced_first_round)

# Specify KNN classifier with tuneable number of neighbours
knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular", neighbors = tune()) |>
  set_engine("kknn") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# Tune odd k values from 1 to 35 to avoid tie votes
k_grid <- tibble(neighbors = seq(from = 1, to = 35, by = 2))

knn_results <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(march_recipe) |>
  add_model(knn_spec) |>
  tune_grid(resamples = march_vfold, grid = k_grid) |>
  collect_metrics()

# Summarize 5-fold CV accuracy and extract the optimal k
cv_accuracies <- knn_results |>
  filter(.metric == "accuracy") |>
  arrange(desc(mean))

cv_accuracies

best_k <- cv_accuracies |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(neighbors)

best_k

# Fit final KNN model using best_k on the full training set
final_knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular", neighbors = best_k) |>
  set_engine("kknn") |>
  set_mode("classification")

final_knn_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(march_recipe) |>
  add_model(final_knn_spec) |>
  fit(data = march_train)

# Predict outcomes on the held-out test set and compute accuracy and confusion matrix
march_predictions <- predict(final_knn_fit, march_test) |>
  bind_cols(march_test)

test_accuracy <- march_predictions |>
  metrics(truth = advanced_first_round, estimate = .pred_class) |>
  filter(.metric == "accuracy")

test_accuracy

march_conf_mat <- march_predictions |>
  conf_mat(truth = advanced_first_round, estimate = .pred_class)

march_conf_mat

Part 6: Discuss your Results (10 points)¶

In this section, you will discuss some interesting findings from your analysis in Part 5

Task 6.1: Discuss your findings (10 points)¶

In 1 to 2 paragraphs (approx. 300 words or less):

  • Summarize what you found from the analysis in Part 5, in relation to your research question of interest.
  • The data science workflow is an iterative process. Discuss if at any point you had to adjust your analysis plan based on the results.
  • Discuss whether this is what you expected, or if anything was surprising.
  • Discuss the impact of the results, and what future questions this could lead to.

Using tournament seed and regular season win percentage in a KNN classifier achieved a test accuracy of 75.38% (395 of 524 teams) with 27 neighbours, well above the 51.9% majority-class baseline. This confirms that pre-tournament seeding and regular season record provide strong predictive signal for first-round advancement in women's college basketball. During the iterative workflow, converting the outcome variable advanced_first_round from logical to factor was required for classification fitting in tidymodels, and I tuned odd k values from 1 to 35 to avoid binary tie votes while keeping normalization restricted to the training split.

The accuracy matched my expectation because seeding already reflects committee strength rankings, and the confusion matrix shows balanced performance across both outcomes (192 true negatives, 203 true positives, 60 false positives, and 69 false negatives). Even so, 129 games were still misclassified, with seeds 7 through 10 accounting for 64 of those errors, where teams are closely matched and seed plus overall win percentage cannot separate narrow differences. Future work could test whether adding conference strength, qualification bid type, or home-court indicator improves predictions in these close middle-seed matchups.
